statement: A square has sides of 4 cm. A rectangle 6 cm long has the same distance all the way round as the square. How wide is the rectangle?

choices.misconception: I gave the side of the square instead of working out the rectangle.
I took one long side away from the distance round and halved what was left, forgetting the other long side.
I halved the distance round and stopped, which gives the length and width added together.
I took one long side away from the distance round and stopped there.

hints: First find the distance round the square.
The square's four sides give the distance round. The rectangle has the same total. Take away its two long sides, and what is left is shared by its two short sides.
The distance round is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm. The two long sides of the rectangle use 6 + 6 = 12 cm of that.

solutions.reliable: The square's distance round is 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 16 cm. The rectangle's two long sides make 6 + 6 = 12 cm, so its two short sides make 16 - 12 = 4 cm, and each one is 2 cm. Check: 6 + 2 + 6 + 2 = 16. The idea to keep: a rectangle has two of each side, so take both long sides away before sharing what is left.
solutions.elegant: Half of the distance round is one length plus one width. Half of 16 is 8, and 8 - 6 = 2 cm. The idea to keep: half the perimeter of a rectangle is length plus width.

whyOnTest: Working backwards from a perimeter needs the idea that each side comes twice, and every wrong choice forgets that somewhere.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
